title: Method Overloading
description: Several methods sharing one name, told apart by what you pass them.

items: Java lets several methods share a name, as long as they take different things.
At each call, Java picks the one whose parameters match the arguments. This is **overloading**.
Without it you would need `greet`, `greetName` and `greetNameTimes`, and have to remember which is which.

steps.note: No arguments. Only one `greet` takes nothing.
So Java jumps into that one.
A `String` and an `int`. Only the third version matches.
The loop prints the greeting three times.

content.title: Watch Java pick by the arguments
content.outro: Three separate methods, one name between them.

content.question: Which `greet` runs for `greet("Mia")`?
options: greet()
greet(String name, int times)
greet(String name)
None: it does not compile
content.explain: One `String` argument matches the version with one `String` parameter.

items: A method's **signature** is its name plus its parameter list: how many, what types, in what order.
Two methods may share a name only if their signatures differ: a different number, type or order of parameters.
Different parameter **names** do not count. Neither does a different **return type**.

items.title: Does not compile
items.code:
static int size(String text)
static double size(String text)
items.text: Same parameters. `error: method size(String) is already defined in class Main`.

items.title: Compiles
items.code:
static int half(int n)
static double half(double n)
items.text: Different parameter types, so every call matches exactly one.

content.title: Return type alone is not enough
content.caption: At the call `size("hello")` there would be no way to know which one you meant, so javac rejects it.

`9` is an int, so it goes to the int version, and whole-number division drops the half. `9.0` is a double, so it goes to the other. Java makes this choice when it compiles, from the types written in your code.

content.question: What does this print?
options: double version: 3.5
int version: 3.5
int version: 3
double version: 3.0
content.explain: `7` is an int, so the int version runs, and `7 / 2` in whole numbers is 3.
content.code:
// using the two half methods above
System.out.println(half(7));

content.value: You Have Used It All Along

content.real: One word, "open", for a door, a jar or a book
content.text: You say "open" and the thing in your hand decides how. `println` works the same way: the argument's type picks the version.

content.caption: `println` has a version for an int, a double, a boolean, a char, a String and more, all sharing one name.

content.value: You never had to think about which print to use. That is the point of overloading: the library author took the trouble so you did not have to.

items: Java has no default parameter values. Overloading is the replacement.
The standard pattern: the short method fills in the default and hands over to the long one.
Only one method holds the real work. Never copy the same loop into both overloads.

content.caption: This pattern scales: `printBar(int)` calls `printBar(int, char)`, which could call `printBar(int, char, String)`. Each overload adds one decision and passes the rest along.

items.title: Same idea
items.text: Both print a score line. One just has an extra detail.

items.title: Different jobs
items.code:
process(total);    // prints a total
process(file);     // deletes a file
items.text: Same name, unrelated behaviour. A cruel trap for the next reader.

content.title: A shared name is a promise

items: Overload only when the methods really do the same job.
Take care with overloads that differ only by `int` and `double`, like `half`. `half(9)` and `half(9.0)` look alike but act differently. Two names may be kinder.

output: Mia: 150 is not a valid score
content.caption: The whole lesson in one program: three calls, two overloads, and one place where the work actually happens, with a boolean helper doing the checking.

content.question: Which pair can NOT both be in one class?
options: int area(int s) and int area(int w, int h)
int area(int s) and double area(int s)
int area(int s) and double area(double s)
void show() and void show(String t)
content.explain: Those two have the same parameter list. A different return type alone does not make a different signature.

practice.question: Write two overloads of area: one taking a single side for a square, one taking a width and a height. Call both.
Write max(int a, int b) and then max(int a, int b, int c). The three-number version must call the two-number one rather than repeating its logic.
Add a one-argument overload of printRow so that printRow(5) draws five stars, while printRow(5, '#') still works.
This does not compile. Read the error, then fix it by giving one of the methods a different parameter list or a different name.

quiz.question: What is method overloading?
options: Several methods with the same name but different parameter lists
Calling a method too many times
A method that calls itself
quiz.explain: Java picks the right one from the arguments at the call site.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT enough to tell two overloads apart?
options: A different return type
A different number of parameters
Different parameter types
quiz.explain: The signature is the name plus the parameter list. `int size(String)` and `double size(String)` clash, and javac says the method is already defined.

quiz.question: Given `int half(int)` and `double half(double)`, what does `half(9)` give?
options: 4, because 9 is an int and whole-number division chops the half off
4.5, because that is the true answer
It is ambiguous and will not compile
quiz.explain: The type you write decides the overload. `half(9.0)` would give 4.5.

quiz.question: How do you get the effect of an optional argument in Java?
options: Write a shorter overload that fills in the default and calls the longer one
Write `int count = 3` in the parameter list
Pass null and check for it
quiz.explain: Only the long version holds the logic. The short one is a single delegating line.

quiz.question: When is overloading a bad idea?
options: When the methods do genuinely different jobs, because the shared name lies
When there are more than two of them
When the parameters have different types
quiz.explain: A shared name promises a shared idea. If the behaviour differs, two clear names are kinder to the reader.
